items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). The simplest SaaS cron scheduler is the one that starts one daily run, records a durable idempotency key, and leaves retries to a worker that can prove the email was already sent. A calendar UI does not solve duplicate reports. The goal is automating a few daily tasks with minimal setup, not building another control plane. TL;DR: use one daily schedule, a small enqueue endpoint, a durable job record, and a retry policy with explicit ownership. Keep the scheduler boring. Put correctness in the job boundary. For a media system, key the run by the report date and recipient group, not by the scheduler's attempt number. daily-report:2026-10-23:regional-editors stays stable across retries. items.title: Edtech Renewal Jobs: Background Queue Workers and Timeout Checkpoints (15-Minute Limit)
items.summary: Short answer: For an edtech renewal reminder, let a cron trigger enqueue checkpointed background queue jobs and keep every worker slice below the 15-minute timeout. A renewal reminder for an edtech account has two clocks: the business deadline and the worker's execution window. The practical answer is to let cron enqueue a small, signed command, then have queue workers process short, checkpointed slices. Keep each lease comfortably below the 15-minute limit, persist the next cursor before acknowledging the message, and make the final send idempotent. You trade a little scheduling latency and storage for recoverability; that is usually the right trade when a missed renewal deadline is harder to explain than a few seconds of delay. I start with the deadline, not with a timer. If a school contract expires at 17:00 local time, the reminder job should calculate a send window and a durable work plan. A cron trigger can wake the planner every five minutes, but it should not carry the whole account scan. Cron is a nudge. The queue is the work ledger. Keep it boring. Megabytes (MB) and gigabytes (GB) are commonly used to describe digital file sizes and storage capacity. However, there is an important distinction between decimal and binary measurements. The basic decimal conversion is simple: GB = MB ÷ 1,000 For example: 500 MB = 0.5 GB 1,000 MB = 1 GB 2,048 MB = 2.048 GB 5,000 MB = 5 GB Let's break down the conversion and look at practical examples for developers. A megabyte and a gigabyte are units used to measure digital information. They are commonly used in: File upload limits Application storage requirements API request and response sizes Database backups Cloud storage plans Software downloads A gigabyte is larger than a megabyte. Under the decimal system: 1 GB = 1,000 MB This is the standard commonly used by storage manufacturers and many storage services. To convert megabytes into gigabytes, divide the MB value by 1,000. items.title: Build an LRU Cache in 25 Lines of JavaScript (Using Nothing but Map)
items.summary: Every time you memoize an API call or cache rendered fragments, you face the same question: what do I throw away when memory fills up? The classic answer is LRU — Least Recently Used: evict the entry nobody has touched for the longest time. Textbook LRU caches use a hash map plus a doubly linked list. In JavaScript you can skip the linked list entirely, because Map remembers insertion order. The first key returned by map.keys() is always the oldest one. If we re-insert a key every time it is read, the front of the Map is automatically the least recently used entry. class LRUCache { constructor(capacity) { if (!Number.isInteger(capacity) || capacity this.capacity) { const oldest = this.map.keys().next().value; this.map.delete(oldest); } return this; } get size() { return this.map.size; } } module.exports = { LRUCache }; get deletes and re-inserts the key, moving it to the "newest" end. set inserts (or refreshes) the key, then evicts map.keys().next().value — the oldest key — if we are over capacity. I'm writing it up anyway, because the kind of bug it fixes is common in any library that wraps one implementation for several frameworks, and nothing in the toolchain catches it. Tiptap is a headless rich-text editor built on ProseMirror. Its drag handle extension shows a grip next to the block you're hovering, so you can drag paragraphs and other blocks around. items.title: I turned C# compiler errors into a game of Snake
items.summary: Every C# editor has a tiny graphics card hiding in it. It only draws three colours, it only refreshes when you type, and most people spend their whole day trying to make it go blank. It's the error squiggle. I built Snake on it. Squiggly is a NuGet package. Add it to a project, create a file with // squiggly on the first line, press Ctrl+. and pick New game: Snake. The snake's head is a red error. Its body is a row of yellow warnings. The food is those faint grey dots you've been ignoring for years. It works in Visual Studio, VS Code (with C# Dev Kit) and Rider, and there's no plugin for any of them. It's just an analyzer. There's Tetris and Minesweeper too, because once you have a screen, you kind of have to. If you've never written one: Roslyn, the C# compiler, lets you plug in your own checks. An analyzer is a class that gets handed your code and can report diagnostics. Those are the same kind of thing as CS0103: The name 'x' does not exist, and your editor draws them as squiggles. The severity picks the colour: errors are red, warnings are yellow (green in Visual Studio), and info shows up as a few grey dots. The other half is code fixes, which is the lightbulb menu. items.title: Node.js Rate-Limited Webhook Subscriptions with 3 Push-Queue Controls
items.summary: A renewal reminder has a business deadline, not merely a delivery deadline. If a subscription webhook is rate-limited at the exact moment the reminder becomes due, the queue must preserve the deadline while refusing to amplify the remote limit. My default design is a three-layer control: an idempotency record, a retry schedule with jitter, and a dead-letter path for work that cannot be completed before its useful window closes. That is the short answer. The interesting part is deciding which clock wins. A queue delay is operational state; the renewal date is business state. I keep those separate, then let a worker make an explicit decision from both. Suppose an account renews at 09:00 UTC. The product wants a reminder 24 hours earlier, and the subscription service accepts only a limited number of webhook deliveries per minute. At 08:00, the worker receives a 429 response. A naive loop sleeps for a fixed interval and tries again. That seems harmless until hundreds of accounts reach the same hour, at which point every worker wakes together and creates a second burst. items.title: Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled vs Promise.race in JavaScript: Differences and When to Use Each (Tested Examples)
items.summary: Promise.all waits for every promise to fulfill and fails fast on the first rejection. Promise.allSettled waits for every promise to finish and always fulfills with an array of {status, value|reason} results. Promise.race settles with whichever promise settles first, success or failure. Use all when one failure should cancel the whole batch, allSettled when you need every outcome, and race for timeouts or "first response wins". MDN's pages for these methods are the official reference. This guide shows the behaviour with real timings I measured on Node.js 24.22.1 (and confirmed the methods exist on Node 20.20.2 and 18.20.8). items.title: Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use in Node.js: 10 Causes and Fixes (Tested on Linux, Windows tips, nodemon)
items.summary: "Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000" means another process is already listening on port 3000, so your Node.js server can't bind to it. The quick fix on Linux or macOS is to find that process with lsof -i :3000 and stop it with kill . On Windows, use netstat -ano | findstr :3000 and then taskkill /PID /F. If you need both servers running, start yours on a different port instead. The Node.js docs on common system errors describe EADDRINUSE as a failed attempt to bind a server to a local address because another server already occupies it. The hard part is working out which server that is, because it's often a copy of your own app that you can't see. items.title: Hold up — I had a great time talking to the RIAA guy
items.summary: Today, I’m talking with Mitch Glazier, who is CEO and chairman of the RIAA. This conversation was a real full-circle moment for me: I was in college when Napster hit, and the RIAA became everyone’s villain for suing kids for downloading music. That was when I decided to go be a copyright lawyer, which set the rest of my career in motion — and Mitch was in the background as a young lawyer at the RIAA working on those cases. items.title: Build a Multilingual React Reflection Portal with GitHub Pages
items.summary: If a daily-content project starts as a folder of JSON files, the first useful web interface does not need a database server. It needs a predictable data shape, a small client-side state model, and a deployment target that can serve static files. This tutorial builds that path with AA Daily Reflections Database, an open-source React portal that publishes English, Spanish, French, and Brazilian Portuguese data as JSON, CSV, and SQLite. The goal is not to reproduce its reflection text here. The goal is to understand the reusable engineering pattern: select a language, select a date, load one static data file, and deploy the result as a static site. Clone the repository, install its Node.js dependencies, run the data-copy step, and build the React app. The portal keeps the selected language and date in localStorage, fetches the matching language JSON from public/data, and uses PUBLIC_URL so the same build can work locally or beneath a GitHub Pages project path. The repository currently targets React 18.2.0 and react-scripts 5.0.1 in package.json. The live site is available on GitHub Pages. items.title: Authentication and Authorization: What's New in .NET 11
items.summary: When it comes to authentication and authorization, .NET 11 focuses on valuable refinements. It addresses key edge cases to enhance security and user experience: a WebSocket that outlives its access token, an authorization attribute that works on one endpoint type but not on another, a passkey list full of identical "Passkey" labels. Let's look at what the newest release brings to authentication and authorization. A SignalR connection can live for hours, while an access token usually doesn't. Until now, you had two unattractive options when the token expired: close the connection and make the client reconnect (missing messages in the gap), or leave it open and keep trusting an identity that is no longer valid. .NET 11 adds a third option: authentication refresh. The client sends the old token over a dedicated /refresh endpoint, and the server swaps the connection's ClaimsPrincipal in place. items.title: .NET 8 and 9 lose support on Nov 10. Your image tags won't tell you which pods run them.
items.summary: Tomorrow, November 10, 2026, .NET 8 and .NET 9 both reach end of support. .NET 8 was the LTS release and .NET 9 the STS one, and they end on the same day. After that, neither gets security patches. .NET 10 is the LTS to move to, supported until November 14, 2028. If you run .NET on Kubernetes, the first question is a boring one, and it's harder than it sounds: which of the containers running right now are actually on 8 or 9? I spent some time on this while building runtime checks for Runtimez, and the image tag turned out to be the least useful place to look. mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0 is easy. The version is right there. But almost nobody runs that image directly. You build your own: FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0 COPY publish/ /app ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "/app/Orders.Api.dll"] and push it as registry.example.com/orders-api:1.42. Now the tag is your app's version, and the .NET version is gone from everything kubectl get pods shows you. The usual next move is kubectl exec and dotnet --list-runtimes. That works until you hit a chiseled image, which has no shell. It also means exec-ing into production pods to answer an inventory question, which I'd rather avoid. Mic

items.summary: Originally published on AppRanker. The Xcode 27 requirement lands in April 2027, and it is not just "bump Xcode and archive." From that month, App Store Connect rejects uploads built with older SDKs, your iOS minimum moves to 15, and the Info.plist key that kept your app out of Liquid Glass stops doing anything. Here is what changes, the commands to audit each app in a few minutes, and a month-by-month plan so the cutoff never blocks a hotfix. Apple announced the rule on September 9, 2026, the same day iOS 27 submissions opened. It applies to every upload, TestFlight builds included, not just App Store releases. Platform From April 2027 iOS and iPadOS iOS & iPadOS 27 SDK or later, deployment target iOS 15 or later tvOS tvOS 27 SDK or later visionOS visionOS 27 SDK or later watchOS watchOS 27 SDK or later macOS apps are not on the list. The exact day has not been published, and an Apple DTS engineer declined to give one on the developer forums. History is a decent guide, though: the Xcode 15 cutoff started on April 29, 2024 and the Xcode 26 cutoff on April 28, 2026. items.title: Building a Production AI Chatbot in Next.js: Architecture and Pitfalls
items.summary: You have a working chat interface in an afternoon. Turning it into a product users pay for takes months. The gap isn't the model: it's conversation history, citations, cost guards, and the boring auth and billing layer nobody talks about. Token-by-token rendering is the baseline. You need SSE or fetch streaming, Markdown rendering mid-stream with code blocks and syntax highlighting, a stop button, regenerate, edit-and-resend, and scroll-to-bottom that respects where the user scrolled. The Vercel AI SDK handles all of this. Don't roll streaming yourself. Not a single chat: a list of chats with a sidebar, new-chat button, rename and delete, folders or categories, search across conversations, pinning, and optional public sharing. Storage is a conversations table with messages linked by conversation_id, indexed by user and updated-at. Production chatbots route across OpenAI GPT-5 for reasoning, Anthropic Claude for long context, Gemini for multimodal, self-hosted Llama or Mistral for privacy, and fine-tunes for specific tasks. It also counts a retried request four times, loses plays when a worker crashes at the wrong moment, and happily lets one script "listen" to a track 2,000 times an hour. So when I built a Spotify-style play count in .NET 10 recently, I didn't start with the counter. I started with the tests that would tell me the counter was lying. items.summary: Futurism reports: While many scientists have long held that Mars is "geologically dead" inside, new research is adding to the growing body of evidence to the contrary. As detailed in a new paper published in the journal Science Advances, an international team of researchers examined data collected by the European and Russian ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter in 2021, which found that Mars is slowly belching hydrogen chloride gas. The researchers suggest this gas is being released from hot magma deep beneath its surface after discovering intriguing new fissures along a massive volcano, indicating the planet may be geologically active after all — or at least it was until relatively recently. The research could have significant implications for the possibility of ancient life on the Red Planet, hinting at a far warmer and thicker atmosphere — and an abundance of liquid water on its surface — in its not-too-distant past.... The team discovered new fissures measuring thousands of feet in length... suggesting ongoing activity underneath the surface. items.title: TypeScript `Map` and `Set` Iteration in 2026: Why `downlevelIteration` Still Breaks Production Builds
items.summary: TypeScript Map and Set Iteration in 2026: Why downlevelIteration Still Breaks Production Builds This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review. TypeScript's downlevelIteration flag determines how the compiler transpiles Map, Set, and array iteration when targeting older JavaScript runtimes. Without it, production builds silently produce broken code that crashes on iterables at runtime. The default behavior downlevels for...of loops to index-based iteration, which fails on objects that implement Symbol.iterator but lack numeric indices. The flag's confusing name compounds the problem. Developers expect "downlevel" to mean "produce simpler code for older targets," but enabling the flag actually generates more complex helper code that checks for Symbol.iterator before falling back to index-based iteration. The flag appears optional until a production build crashes with "Object is not iterable" on a perfectly valid Map.values() call. items.summary: São 3h12 da manhã. A API de pedidos começa a devolver erro 500, o health check fica vermelho e ninguém está olhando. Quando o time chega às 8h, o problema já virou reclamação de cliente, e a primeira hora do dia é gasta só para entender o que aconteceu. Esse é o cenário em que um agente de IA de plantão faz sentido. Ele não substitui o time nem sai reiniciando servidor por conta própria. Ele faz a triagem: percebe o problema, investiga com as ferramentas que você liberou, junta as evidências, abre o incidente com um diagnóstico e, se for o caso, pede autorização para agir. Neste artigo eu mostro como construir esse agente em .NET 10, rodando 24 horas por dia, usando o gpt-5.4-mini no Microsoft Foundry. E falo de um assunto que quase ninguém aborda até tomar o primeiro erro 429 em produção: as cotas do Foundry. Num chat, tem uma pessoa do outro lado. Se a resposta demorar, falhar ou sair estranha, ela percebe. Num agente que roda sozinho de madrugada, ninguém percebe nada. items.title: Message queues and asynchronous processing, explained through a trip to the dry cleaner
items.summary: Why Your Bank App Says "Successful" Before the SMS Arrives When you drop your clothes at the dry cleaner, nobody asks you to wait at the counter while they wash, dry and iron everything. They hand you a ticket and say, "We'll call you when it's ready." You go about your day. The work still happens. It just doesn't happen while you stand there waiting. That simple idea is behind one of the most important patterns in modern software. It's the reason your banking app can say "Transfer successful" in about a second, while the SMS alert, the receipt and the rewards points arrive a few moments later. Engineers call it asynchronous processing, and the tool that makes it work is the message queue. In this article, I'll explain what a message queue is, why payment systems depend on it, and the rules experienced engineers follow so that nothing gets lost in between. When you tap "Send" on a transfer, a lot happens. But not all of it needs to happen before you see a result. items.title: I Expected string.Create to Be Faster. It Just Stopped Allocating.
items.summary: I had a hot loop stamping out order keys — little strings like ORD-0000042-US — a couple million of them per refresh. The code was the most boring thing in the file, so of course that's where the allocation profiler kept parking. I figured I'd reach for string.Create, the usual "stop allocating intermediate strings" move, get my speedup, and go home. I got half of what I expected. The interesting half. Here's the code I started with. It's what most of us write without thinking, and honestly it's fine: static string ConcatKey(int id, string region) => "ORD-" + id.ToString("D7") + "-" + region; Clean, readable, obviously correct. But look at what it allocates. There's the final string, sure, you can't avoid that one. And then there's id.ToString("D7") — a whole separate seven-character string that exists for one reason: to be copied into the concatenation and then immediately thrown away. Every single call makes one. Two million calls, two million little garbage strings. So the plan was string.Create, which hands you a Span over the final string's buffer and lets you write the characters in directly. items.title: My Struct Update Copied 64 Bytes Twice
items.summary: I had a physics step that walked a List every frame and nudged each body's position by its velocity. Simple loop, nothing exotic. And the profiler kept pointing at it with more weight than three lines of double addition had any right to carry. The arithmetic wasn't the problem. The copies were. Here's the thing I'd forgotten. When you index into a List of structs, you don't get the element. You get a copy of it. So this doesn't even compile: world[i].X += world[i].Vx; The compiler stops you cold: error CS1612: Cannot modify the return value of 'List .this[int]' because it is not a variable Which is actually the compiler being honest. If it let you write that, you'd be mutating a throwaway copy and the real element would sit there unchanged, and you'd spend an afternoon wondering why your bodies never move. items.title: British people don’t trust Palantir – it’s not too late to reverse the NHS’s dependence on it | Ben Coleman
items.summary: We can’t allow our health data to be locked into the control of a US tech firm. It won’t be easy, but next spring the job of clawing it back must begin Ben Coleman is Labour MP for Chelsea and Fulham and a member of the health and social care committee Next March, Palantir’s £330m contract to run NHS England’s federated data platform (FDP) ends. Ministers must decide by Christmas whether to extend it. They should move on from Palantir, and transition to new suppliers that put the NHS in full control of its technology and patient data. I sit on the health and social care committee. In June, we recommended no extension – people don’t trust Palantir, its benefits are contested and other tools could deliver the same or similar advantages. items.title: iOS Silent Push Notifications That Actually Arrive: content-available, Priority 5 and the Throttling Rules
items.summary: Silent push notifications (Apple calls them background notifications) are the push you send when you don't want to show anything. You just want the app to wake up, fetch new data, refresh a cache or sync a record. They're also the push type developers most often swear "doesn't work." Usually it does work. It just follows rules that visible alerts don't. This guide covers the exact payload and headers, the app-side code, and the reasons a silent push gets delayed or dropped. A silent push is a payload with content-available set to 1 and no alert, sound or badge: { "aps": { "content-available": 1 }, "type": "sync", "since": "2026-11-09T04:00:00Z" } Anything outside aps is your own data and is handed to the app. Keep the total under 4 KB. If you add an alert to the same payload, it's no longer a silent push. It becomes a visible notification that also happens to wake the app, and it follows the visible-alert rules instead. When you call APNs over HTTP/2, a background notification needs these headers: Header Value apns-push-type background apns-priority 5 apns-topic your app's bundle ID Two rules matter here: apns-push-type must be background. items.summary: Be careful with the file .claude/settings.local.json, warns The Hacker News: Passwords and API keys that developers typed into commands they approved in Claude Code are sitting in public GitHub repositories, where anyone can read them. When a user selects "Yes, and don't ask again," Anthropic's AI coding assistant can save the command, word-for-word, including the secret, in a project settings file. Software security company Apiiro said that 1,122 public copies of that file hold at least one secret, though it did not test whether any still work. One company the researchers notified earlier this week confirmed its key had been live... Removing [the file] from a project does not undo the leak, because older versions stay in git history and in forks of the repository. The researchers' advice is to rotate first: change every password, token, and key the file has ever held, then clean up... Claude Code tries to keep the file out of git. The first time it writes the file in a git repository, it adds the file to the user's global git excludes, its settings documentation says. items.title: Do Data Centers Have a Smaller Effect on Electricity Prices Than We Think?
items.summary: "According to a new study by researchers at Harvard University and the University of Pennsylvania, data centers are probably having only a small effect on residential electricity prices," reports the Washington Post. "The researchers calculated that these operations were responsible for just 4% of the utility rate increases over the last five years..." There are certainly some areas — like in Pennsylvania, Virginia, Ohio and other states covered by grid operator PJM — where data centers have skyrocketed demand, pushing some costs onto residential customers. But multiple studies by different researchers and organizations have failed to find a strong connection between data centers and the overall trajectory of U.S. electricity prices in recent years. Another analysis earlier this year by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that, between 2010 and 2024, data centers increased average electricity prices for residential customers by just 2.1%. The GTA 6 list ships empty. That sounds odd for a cheats app, but an empty list with a clear reason is more honest than a full one made of guesses. items.title: Breathe as One: a two-phone co-op game you win by breathing together
items.summary: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge Breathe as One is a little co-op game for two people and two iPhones. You win by breathing together. You sit across from each other with your phones propped up, front cameras facing you. Each phone only watches its own player. The SmartSpectra SDK picks up the rise and fall of your chest and turns it into a live wave, and the two phones swap those waves over a private nearby connection. So both screens show the same thing: your breath in blue and your partner's in coral. As you settle into the same rhythm, the two lines drift toward each other's color until they melt into one lilac line. Getting there is the whole game. A game takes a few minutes and has three rounds: Follow the Tide (45 s). A white wave rolls across the screen at 6 breaths a minute, and you both ride it. No Leader (60 s). The wave goes away and you have to find each other without a guide. It's harder than it sounds, and it's my favorite part. Heart Meet (45 s). items.title: How to Stamp a Transparent PNG Logo Across a Batch of Photos in Swift
items.summary: If you need the same logo on thirty photos, the boring bugs show up immediately: the mark looks huge on a 12-megapixel still and timid on a 48-megapixel one, the PNG’s transparent background turns into a grey box, or the edges of the logo go muddy because the alpha channel was applied twice. This post walks through a small UIKit pipeline that loads a transparent PNG, draws each photo, then draws the logo at a size tied to the photo’s shorter side, inset by a percentage of the frame. I’m writing it from the seat of someone who builds BatchMark, an on-device batch photo app; the batch watermark path is where this idea lives in the product. The code below is a teaching extract, not a dump of the app. People say “put the logo in the corner” and mean three separate decisions: How large is it, visually? Not “200 pixels,” because 200 pixels is a different object on a 4032-pixel-wide photo than on a 8064-pixel-wide one. How far is it from the edges? A 40-point inset looks generous on a screenshot and lost on a full-resolution export. How does it sit on top of the photo? The PNG already has transparency. items.title: Is there a free way to hide Instagram Reels on iPhone and keep DMs? Why iOS makes it hard
items.summary: iOS doesn't let any app change the official Instagram app, so the free way to hide Reels on iPhone and keep DMs is to use Instagram's website inside an app that controls its own view, such as minulo, where hiding Reels is free and DMs, group chats included, keep working. Disclosure up front: I'm the developer of minulo. What I say about other apps comes only from their App Store descriptions and help pages, and the page linked at the end lists the sources. The iOS part below is a general overview of how the platform works, not a deep dive into any one API. If you write iOS code, you may have had this thought: "I'll build a tiny tool that removes the Reels tab from Instagram." You open Xcode on a Saturday and soon hit the wall: there is no API for it that an App Store app could use. Here is why, and what is left. Sandboxing. Every iOS app runs in its own sandbox. It gets its own container for files, and it can't read another app's memory, inject code into it, or draw over its interface. items.title: Fixing a streaming SwiftUI chat hang: stable scroll anchors and local/cloud cancellation
items.summary: In a SwiftUI reference app, streamed model output and illustrated answer cards repeatedly change the transcript’s height. The assistant uses Apple Foundation Models when available, with a consent-controlled online fallback. A reproduced layout hang led to changes in both rendering and task lifetime. The failure Opening “Ask guide” from an entry could leave the process hung at roughly 99% CPU. The sampled main thread repeatedly hit SwiftUI lazy-stack placement/graph updates, and the observed process footprint reached 1.1 GB. Reopening returned to the same hung process. A UI reproduction also timed out while querying the app. The transcript combined lazy height estimation, a scroll target on a growing answer, animated scrolling, and frequent streamed-text updates. This was a reproduced layout hang; I wouldn't generalize it into “LazyVStack is bad for chat.” What changed A measured VStack replaced the lazy transcript stack. Every exchange gets a separate fixed-height anchor before its changing content. Inserting an exchange triggers one nonanimated scroll to that anchor. items.title: Building Ping Hunt: a GPS treasure hunt app for iOS and Android
items.summary: Looking for a treasure hunt near you? Ping Hunt turns an ordinary walk into a GPS scavenger hunt — you follow waypoints to real places and match what you see against the viewfinder. I have been building Ping Hunt as a small solo mobile project, and you can find it here: https://www.pinghunt.com It is available on both platforms: iOS: Ping Hunt on the App Store Android: Ping Hunt on Google Play How it works Open the app and pick a hunt near you. Follow the GPS coordinates to each waypoint. Match the view in the camera viewfinder to unlock the next step. No setup, no library of pre-made caches to manage — you just open the app and play the hunt that is right in front of you. Modern phones already know exactly where you are and what you are looking at. The hard part was never the GPS; it was turning "you are here" into something that feels like play. So Ping Hunt removes the busywork of classic geocaching — logging finds, maintaining a profile, managing dozens of tiny icons in a map — and keeps the part that is fun: walking somewhere because there is a small mystery waiting there. items.title: How I built a Wordle-style daily puzzle in SwiftUI (no backend)
items.summary: I recently shipped Gemdoku: Daily Block Puzzle, a 9×9 block puzzle for iPhone. The core feature is a Wordle-style Daily Challenge: every player in the world gets the same goal, the same move limit and the exact same sequence of pieces each day. It turned out to be a fun little engineering problem. Here's how it works under the hood, all in plain Swift and SwiftUI, with no backend. The obvious way to give everyone the same puzzle is to generate it on a server. I didn't want a backend. The game is fully offline, has no accounts and collects no data. So the daily puzzle has to be derived, not downloaded. The trick is a seeded random number generator. Swift's RandomNumberGenerator protocol makes this easy. Incredibly, I am far from alone. This is not some strange protest against the popular retailer. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills. These days, of course, most video games are bought as digital copies that download straight to your PC or console on the day of release. You don’t even have to get out of bed to start playing. items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

items.title: ‘Apologies for any confusion!’: how to write the perfect passive-aggressive email
items.summary: In a survey, ‘just to be clear’ came out as the most loathed phrase. But I think I can do better A new contender for the most passive-aggressive email phrase has emerged. “Just to be clear” was chosen by 52% of desk jockeys in a survey by email verification company ZeroBounce, closely followed by the perennial pass-ag fave, “per my last email” (40%), which tied with the identical-in-intent “as previously discussed”. Further down the list came “for future reference” and “kindly note”. If you ask me, these all verge on actual aggressive. Imagine saying “just to be clear” out loud to another person: that’s a conversational poke in the ribs, isn’t it? It’s the kind of thing you unleash 10 minutes into an ill-tempered wrangle with your home insurance company about inflated renewal premiums. “Kindly note” is even worse – it’s a phrase from an angry message on the office kitchen wall about microwave abuse. items.title: The surprising leadership dynamics in agent swarms (17 minute read)
items.summary: Agent swarms are groups of agents that work together to accomplish a task. Researchers created an experiment in which eight agents from four different models worked together to resolve simulated outages to understand how agents organize themselves in a swarm without a designated leader. They discovered two factors that could influence an agent's potential leadership: the agent's underlying models, and the order in which their name was listed in a prompt. This suggests that even seemingly minor details in how an agent swarm is configured can affect how agents coordinate.
